13824-the-national-preacher-vol-2-no-7-d:
Austin Dickinson edited The National Preacher as a monthly of original sermons. This December 1827 number, volume two, number seven, prints sermons by Dr. Leland and Mr. Baldwin. Postage rates on the cover show how the magazine travelled by mail across the young republic. An appeal to clergy proposes a new periodical of pastoral sketches.

The sermons stress faith, duty, and the danger of lowering divine truth to human taste. Preachers warn against moulding doctrine to suit unholy inclinations. The language is earnest and direct, aimed at ministers and devout readers. The issue captures American evangelical preaching before the Civil War. It also shows early religious publishing in action.
18241-tea-cup-reading-and-fortune-tellin:
A Highland Seer wrote this guide to fortune telling by tea leaves, published in New York by George Sully and Company with ten illustrations. The book teaches the art of divination from the leaves left in a cup, and it treats the practice as a skill with rules, not as mere guesswork. China tea, the author says, works best, since Indian tea and cheap mixtures leave too much dust and twig fragments.

Chapters cover the ritual and method of using the teacup, general principles for reading the cup, an alphabetical list of symbols with their meanings, specimen cups with interpretations, and omens. Ten figures show cups to study. Readers get a complete manual for the parlor art: how to pour, how to read shapes, and how to turn a tea party into a fortune.
18329-the-national-preacher-vol-2-no-6-n:
One monthly number of The National Preacher, volume two, number six, for November 1827, edited by Rev. Austin Dickinson in New York. The periodical promised one long sermon, or two of moderate length, in each number, printed on superfine paper and sold for a cent and a half postage within a hundred miles. This number opens with Sermon Twenty-Five, from Rev. Mr. Patton.

Subscribers in city and country were asked to send payments to the editor or his agents, and readers who got the number free were asked to pass it on. The issue is a small window on American religion in the 1820s: preaching by living ministers, carried by post, read at home, and shared hand to hand. Its value today lies in that plain record of pulpit and parish life.
21943-peter-schlemihl:
A man sells his shadow to a stranger in Peter Schlemihl, Adelbert von Chamisso's famous German tale, Englished here by Sir John Bowring in 1861. George Cruikshank's plates show Schlemihl giving his shadow away, the bargain that ruins and remakes him. The translator's notice tells how Adelung promised him at Petersburg: read it, and you will translate it. He did, with only trifling changes.

Bowring calls the story a moral one and leaves its lessons to the reader's own eye. Chamisso, a French-born German poet and botanist, wrote the tale in a few weeks of 1813. It became a European classic, and Schlemihl a byword for the luckless man. Shadowless, Peter wanders the world learning what men truly prize. The fable still reads freshly.
37624-count-bru-hl:
Count Bruhl is a historical novel by Joseph Kraszewski, issued in English in the Lotus Library of Continental fiction. The series list around it names works by Zola, Tolstoy, Flaubert, and Daudet, each in foolscap size with gilt top edge and a bookmark. Count Bruhl stands among such titles as Cagliostro and Co and The Diamond Necklace.

The frontispiece shows riders pushing on at a smart trot. Kraszewski was Poland's most prolific novelist, and his tales of the Saxon court were famed at home. The novel takes its hero from the court of Saxony and Poland, where Bruhl rose as the all-powerful minister of his king. Intrigue, favour, and fall make its matter. The English dress in this series brought many Continental novels to American readers at a dollar a volume.
43382-harper-s-young-people-november-16-:
Harper's Young People, volume two, number fifty-five, is an illustrated weekly dated Tuesday, November 16, 1880, priced four cents. Rose Terry Cooke's story The Fox-Skin Coat leads the number. Doctor Putnam ties coarse socks over his boots for a dark cold night call, telling his wife Jenny not to fret.

Sam, almost sixteen, fetches and lights the old tin lantern promptly, hangs it by the wagon seat, and tucks the worn buffalo robe carefully round his father. The air is bitter, no star visible, wind northeast right in the driver's face, the boy reports at the door. A country doctor's life is hard in all weather and seasons. Children got stories, pictures, and verse weekly.
43434-harper-s-young-people-november-23-:
Harper Young People of November twenty third, eighteen eighty, is one week sheet for youth. The Harper house of New York put it out at four cents a copy. Year two, sheet fifty six, is the mark on its front leaf. A front cut shows the boy Samuel at prayer in the shrine. The lead tale tells the youth of Samuel by Bradford Peirce, a church man.

Peirce tells how Hannah prayed long for a son in a hill town. The name Samuel means asked of God in the old tongue, he notes. At age two or three she left the boy at the great tent shrine. There priest men taught him for a life of God work in Israel. Each year his dam brought him a new robe as a love gift.
43474-harper-s-young-people-november-30-:
Harper Young People, number fifty seven, is an illustrated weekly for youth. Harper and Brothers of New York issued it on November thirtieth eighteen eighty. The price was four cents, or a dollar fifty a year in advance. Its lead tale is A Good Day Work, by Frank Taylor.

Eddie Stevens rushes in with news that Bill Joyce has run away. Bill would not pick the widow apples, took her money, and fled. His mother grieves alone, with a mortgaged place and a burnt barn. Eddie tale draws grammar fixes from his mother as he tells it. Say saw, not seen, she tells the boy in mid story twice.
44595-harper-s-young-people-december-14-:
Harper's Young People for December 14, 1880, is volume 2, number 59 of the weekly from Harper and Brothers of New York, priced at four cents. The lead piece is 'My Sister's Grapes' by the author of 'John Halifax, Gentleman'. Its subject is Uncle Dick, who lived with his brother's widow Emma and her many children, though he could scarcely be said to live anywhere, being always on the move.

Aunt Emma did not think Uncle Dick a gentleman: he never would take his position in the world, avoiding her balls and dinner parties. The boys admired his shooting-jacket, knickerbockers, and Panama hat, and had no doubt of him. He had amassed two fortunes, losing the first at about twenty-five: he went to sleep a rich man and by daylight was a beggar. The story unfolds as the boys ply him with questions while the fish refuse to bite.
44596-harper-s-young-people-december-28-:
Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for children, in its New Year number dated Tuesday, December 28, 1880, price four cents. The front page greets the incoming year as a little fur-clad figure knocking at every door at midnight, laden with promises.

Readers are urged to welcome Master Eighteen Eighty-One warmly. The first story, Prince Charlie by Katherine Kameron, opens after Christmas with twins Allan and Jessie studying their mother's gift, a picture of the children of Charles the First. The tallest boy in scarlet velvet holds a tiny tot by the hand while spaniels crouch at their feet. Children get stories, pictures, and holiday warmth in the Harper manner.
56386-the-catholic-world-vol-23-april-18:
The Catholic World, a monthly magazine of general literature and science, fills this file with its twenty third volume, running from April to September 1876. The Catholic Publication House of New York issued it from Warren Street. Six monthly numbers stand bound together, and the contents list runs to scores of pieces, from essays and reviews to tales told in parts.

Among them stand pieces on Catholics in the American Revolution, on Charles Carroll of Carrollton, and on the Catholic Church in the United States across its first hundred years. Easter in Saint Peter's at Rome, the Irish Home Rule Movement, and German journalism widen the range. The volume shows an American Catholic monthly marking the nation's centennial year in its own terms.
870-the-love-of-ulrich-nebendahl:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this tale of Ulrich Nebendahl, a German student whose love troubles the Herr Professor and his circle. The story, published in 1908, follows Ulrich through the hopes and humiliations of first love, in a university town where books and beer mix with romance.

Jerome writes with warmth for young love and with humour for the elders who watch it. His tone is gentle, never mocking, and the tale ends in the bittersweet key of youth. The piece suits readers who enjoy Jerome's softer stories, where a small love affair becomes a picture of a whole world.
britannica-1911-suhl:
Suhl, a gun town of Thuringia, is drawn in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Lauter stream on a wooded forest slope. Erfurt lies twenty-nine miles north-east by rail from the town. In 1905 its folk came to near fourteen thousand in count. Smiths of Suhl are named as far back as the ninth century.

Their fame peaked in the years from 1550 to 1634. South German knights prized Suhl swords and Suhl armour most high. Arms for wars with the Turks came from its shops in bulk. New breech guns hurt the town as rival towns took its trade. Great works still turn out firearms, side arms, and machines there. A salt spring by the Domberg hill may have named the town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-nirsch:
Joseph Nirschl was a Bavarian theologian who specialized in the Church Fathers. Born at Durchfurth in 1823, he was ordained in 1851, took a theology doctorate at Munich in 1854, and taught Christian doctrine at Passau. In 1862 he became professor of church history and patrology, the study of the Fathers, and in 1879 he moved to Würzburg.

His chief work was a three-volume textbook of patrology and patristics from 1881 to 1885. He also wrote on Augustine's teaching on evil, on the Immaculate Conception, and on St. Ignatius of Antioch, whose letters he translated into German with the catecheses of St. Cyril of Jerusalem. He defended the genuineness of pseudo-Dionysius and King Abgar's letter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neusohl:
Neusohl is a diocese in Hungary, founded in 1776 by Maria Theresa. Cardinal Peter Pazmany had already planned four new sees to relieve Gran, including Neusohl, but that project lapsed in 1636. Instead four Jesuit colleges rose at Kassa, Neusohl, Kossy and Safron. After the Jesuit suppression, the diocese project revived.

On 7 December 1775 Maria Theresa told Gran's chapter of the decision and asked what revenues it would assign. Royal decision founded the diocese on 11 January 1776, and the papal decree appeared on 13 March. Baron Franz Berchtold, first bishop from 1776 to 1793, held the first canonical visitation from 1778 to 1785. His material efforts failed, and the great fire of 1782, which destroyed the episcopal residence, so harmed the see that Joseph II considered giving it up. The entry follows its bishops, seminary, lyceum and archdeaneries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nikolaus-von-:
Vienna theologian Nikolaus von Dinkelsbühl, born around 1360, led his university and spoke for Austria at Constance. A master by 1390, he taught philosophy, mathematics, and physics, served as dean and rector, and took his theology doctorate in 1409.

Canon of Saint Stephen's from 1405, he acted as ambassador for university and prince, represented Duke Albert V at the Council of Constance, and preached on ending the schism. His sermons and theological writings circulated widely, and he died at Mariazell in 1433. He declined re-election as rector in 1409, though he had served the university in 1405.
chamisso-peter-schlemihl:
A man sells his shadow to a gray stranger for a purse that never empties, and learns what the bargain costs. Adelbert von Chamisso's Peter Schlemihl, from 1814, appears here in English translation. Without a shadow, Peter finds every door in society quietly closed to him.

The tale reads like a fairy story and aches like a confession. Wealth without belonging turns to ashes in his hands, and love slips beyond his reach. Chamisso, himself a French-born exile in Germany, knew the outsider's position from inside. The classic fable of selling one's soul for gold gains unusual melancholy in his telling. It remains one of the great short works of German Romanticism.
doe-osti-3019242-jump-into-stem-2018-202:
Nehemiah Emaikwu, Kim Trenbath, Caroline Hazard, and five colleagues at the National Laboratory of the Rockies reviewed a student competition in NLR/TP-5500-97578, February 2026. JUMP Into STEM ran from 2018 to 2025. College teams tackled building-energy challenges set by the laboratory. One track pushed the envelope, literally: wall retrofit designs for existing homes. Another took up high-performance HVAC, including electric and dual-fuel systems. Each year's challenge asked students to design for real buildings and real grids.

The report pairs highlights with implementation guidance. Organizers at other institutions can lift the challenge structures, judging approaches, and timelines wholesale. Buildings and their grid interactions drive a large share of national energy use, as the text notes. A competition that trains students on that interface is workforce development in disguise. Seven years of challenges give the guidance unusual depth: what worked, what flopped, and what to change next time.
tea-cup-reading-and-fortune-telling-by-t: Tea-Cup Reading and Fortune-Telling by Tea Leaves is by a Highland Seer. George Sully and Company of New York issued the book. Ten plates of cups support the text. The parts first set out the roots of the art. They then give the rite and method of using the cup. Broad rules for reading the cup come next. A long A-to-Z list of signs gives their meanings. Sample cups are then worked out in full. A part on omens closes the book.
the-love-of-ulrich-nebendahl:
Jerome K. Jerome's The Love of Ulrich Nebendahl was published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1909, from a 1904 copyright. The story opens in a Saxon village, where the pastor, Herr Pfarrer Winckelmann, is troubled most of all by Ulrich's bachelor state. As father of the village, he feels bound to see his children marry well, and he urges Ulrich that keeping the hearth fire alive is a citizen's duty.

Over beer, the pastor recalls that at Ulrich's age he already had two boys and a girl. Ulrich answers dreamily that his heart always goes out to the little ones. The pastor then names a candidate: Elsa, good, pious, and economical, whose price is above rubies. Ulrich's face lights at her name, and Jerome lets a matchmaking talk carry the romance's start.
the-national-preacher-vol-2-no-6-nov-182:
Volume 2, No. 6 of The National Preacher, dated November 1827, is present here only as a sermon heading, title page, and subscription notices, so the sermon itself does not appear. Sermon XXV, by the Rev. Mr. Patton, heads the number. The magazine's subtitle promises original monthly sermons from living ministers, edited by the Rev. Austin Dickinson of New York.

A special notice tells subscribers in city and country to send payments to the editor or a named agent, adding that candid men need not be told twice. Postage is stated at one and a half cents under a hundred miles and two and a half cents beyond. J. and J. Harper printed the number at 82 Cliff Street, New York.
the-national-preacher-vol-2-no-7-dec-182:
Volume 2, No. 7 of The National Preacher, dated December 1827, is present here only as title matter and a publisher's proposal, so its two sermons do not appear. Sermons XXVI, by the Rev. Dr. Leland, and XXVII, by the Rev. Mr. Baldwin, are named at the head. The magazine, edited by the Rev. Austin Dickinson in New York, printed original monthly sermons from living ministers.

Most of the pages shown propose a new periodical, The American Pastor's Journal, to be filled with sketches of real characters and striking facts furnished chiefly by clergymen. Its fourteen planned topics range from instances of very early piety and cases of conviction to death-bed scenes of Christians, backsliders, and infidels.
